extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedy performers/organizers, and researchers interested in roast comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive norms for the comedic genre 'roast' — how roasts are structured, what distinguishes them from ordinary insults, and cultural/production considerations for staging or evaluating roasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a roast
rubrics_metrics.description: A roast is a form of insult comedy in which a specific individual, a guest of honor, is subjected to jokes at their expense, as well as genuine praise and tributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry defines the genre: insults are coupled with praise/tributes; anyone mocked in this way is said to have been 'roasted'. Use this definition to distinguish roast-format events from other comedic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of roastee's good humor (consent implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption is that the roastee can take the jokes in good humor and not as serious criticism or insult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent or at least an expectation of consent is central: comedians stress that a true roast requires the consent of the target. If the target cannot or will not take the jokes in stride, the event departs from the roast tradition and risks harm or controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix of insult and tribute (balance/tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts combine biting humor with affectionate tribute — jokes at the honoree's expense are interwoven with genuine praise and tributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining a balance between insult and tribute is a core normative criterion: televised roasts and successful events preserve the tradition's spirit by combining affection with biting remarks. Being 'too insulting' relative to context or audience is repeatedly cited as causing controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and audience framing
rubrics_metrics.description: A roast typically occurs with the roastee surrounded by friends, fans, and well-wishers; there is an expectation of a permissive, familiar audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context determines acceptability — private club roasts, celebrity roasts, and formal-event mockery (e.g., hosts who good-naturedly mock attendees) each have different norms. Organizers should account for the audience makeup and whether participants are insiders or public figures; violating expectations invites backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from harassment and online 'roasting'
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasting on social media (where a person asks others to mock them) exists, but such mockery, even when solicited, has caused controversy and can be considered cyberbullying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solicited nature of online 'roast' requests is a key factor but does not automatically make the activity acceptable. Platform norms, power dynamics, and the severity of insults determine whether behavior is roast-style humor or harassment; organizers/moderators should be cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and responsibility of the roastmaster/host
rubrics_metrics.description: The host of the event is called the roastmaster; the roastmaster plays a coordinating role and sets the tone for the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roastmaster's duties implicitly include managing pacing, speaker order, and tone to preserve the roast's balance between insult and tribute. High-profile roastmasters (or perceived failures of moderation) are often focal points in controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure/format conventions (turn-taking, dais, televised vs. live variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts often feature a dais of comedians and celebrities who take turns roasting the honoree; formats vary across live clubs, televised specials, roast-battle competitions, and web seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventional staging (turn-taking, prepared jokes, tributes) defines audience expectations. Different media adapt the format (e.g., Comedy Central celebrity roasts, 'Roast Battle' competitions, Chinese seasonal Roast! with weekly victims), and producers should select a format that matches audience expectations and broadcast standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and national adaptation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to adapt the American roast format to other countries have produced varied results and sometimes controversy (e.g., British, Indian, Chinese, Australian adaptations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should consider local sensibilities, broadcasting standards, and legal/cultural norms when adapting roast material; what is acceptable in one market may provoke backlash in another (cited examples include the AIB Knockout controversy and varying international roast productions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness in political and formal contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Roast-like mockery appears at political dinners (e.g., Alfred E. Smith Memorial Foundation Dinner, White House Correspondents' Dinner), where candidates and officials sometimes roast each other or themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political settings carry heightened scrutiny: biting remarks at such events have historically attracted media attention and controversy. Comedians and hosts in political contexts must weigh free expression against potential reputational or institutional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for controversy and public reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts have produced controversy when perceived as too insulting, distasteful, sexist, offending, or humiliating; videos or segments have been removed or criticized for crossing lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers and performers should anticipate public reaction, especially for televised or widely distributed roasts; past incidents (removal of videos, critical media attention) illustrate the reputational risk of material judged to exceed acceptable boundaries.
